title: Inference with evidence
examples: How do I know if a character is sad without the book telling me?
What is the difference between guessing and inferring?
Do I have to find the exact sentence that proves my point?

explain.say: Today we are learning to make inferences from texts. An inference is a smart guess you make. You use clues from the text and what you already know.
First, we look for clues in the writing. Clues are details the author gives you. These details help guide your thinking process.

items: Step 1: Find clues in the text

draw.text: Clues are details in the text.

explain.say: Next, you use your own knowledge to make sense. This is what you already know about the world. It helps you understand the clues better.
To make a strong inference, you must quote evidence. This means you must point to the exact words that helped you guess. This makes your guess strong.

draw.text: Quote evidence to support your guess.

explain.say: For example, if the text says the boy ran fast and tripped, you might infer he was running from something. You quote the running and tripping.

items: Text: Boy ran fast and tripped

explain.say: In real life, you use this when you see someone acting strangely. If a friend keeps looking at their phone and not talking, you can infer they are busy.

draw.text: Friend looking at phone, not talking.

faq.q: What is the difference between inferring and guessing?
faq.a: Guessing is just picking something randomly. Inferring uses clues from the text and your knowledge to make a thoughtful guess.
asks: Is inference the same as guessing?
How is inferring different from just guessing?

faq.q: Do I have to find the exact sentence that proves my point?
faq.a: Yes, always try to point to the text. Quoting evidence makes your inference much stronger and easier to prove.
asks: Can I just say what I think?
Do I need to use direct quotes?

faq.q: What if the clues are confusing?
faq.a: If the clues are confusing, it might mean the author wants you to think about it more. You can state that the evidence is unclear.
asks: What if the text is vague?
Can I say I am unsure?

faq.q: Can I use my own life experiences?
faq.a: Yes, your life experiences are part of your background knowledge. They help you understand what the author means by the clues.
asks: Is my personal life knowledge okay to use?
Can I bring in things from my own life?

faq.q: Does the text always give me enough clues?
faq.a: Sometimes the text gives just enough clues. Your job is to connect those small pieces of information together logically.
asks: Will the author always give me the answer?
Is it always clear what I should infer?

facts: An inference is a conclusion reached on the basis of evidence and reasoning.
You must combine textual clues with your existing knowledge to infer.
To support your inference, you must quote specific evidence from the text.
Inferring is a skill that helps you read between the lines.

quiz.say: The character kept looking at the clock and sighed loudly. What can you infer?

options.show: The character was angry at someone.
options.say: The character was angry at someone.

options.show: The character was bored or waiting for something.
options.say: The character was bored or waiting for something.

quiz.why: The sigh and clock-watching suggest passing time slowly, which means boredom or waiting.

wrong.0: Running late usually involves checking a schedule, not just sighing at the clock.
wrong.1: Anger usually involves more visible signs than just looking at the time.
wrong.3: While sighing can mean sadness, the clock focus points more toward time passing slowly.

quiz.say: If a story mentions it is snowing heavily and people are wearing thick coats, what can you infer?

options.show: The people are going to sleep.
options.say: The people are going to sleep.

options.show: The people are going on a picnic.
options.say: The people are going on a picnic.

quiz.why: Snow and thick coats both point directly to low temperatures in the environment.

wrong.0: This inference does not connect the clues of snow and coats.
wrong.2: The text mentions snow, which can happen at any time of day.
wrong.3: Picnics are usually associated with warmer, nicer weather.

quiz.say: The author writes, "The muddy paw prints led away from the cabin." What does this suggest about the animal?
quiz.show: Muddy paw prints away from cabin.

options.show: The animal was afraid of the cabin.
options.say: The animal was afraid of the cabin.

options.show: The animal left the cabin recently.
options.say: The animal left the cabin recently.

options.show: The animal lives in the cabin.
options.say: The animal lives in the cabin.

quiz.why: The prints are muddy, showing they were made recently when the ground was wet, and they lead away, showing departure.

wrong.0: The text only mentions paw prints, not their size, so we cannot guess the size.
wrong.1: While possible, the evidence only shows movement away, not the reason for the movement.
wrong.3: The prints are shown leading away from the cabin, suggesting departure, not residence.
